Read About Auckland

A city built on fifty volcanoes, spread across two harbours on two different seas, that spent a century arguing about what to call itself.

A city standing on its own volcanoes

Auckland sits on top of an active volcanic field. This is not a metaphor and not ancient history — the Auckland Volcanic Field has been erupting on and off for roughly 200,000 years, and geologists are confident it will erupt again, they just cannot say where or when. More than fifty scoria cones, craters, and lava fields are scattered across the isthmus, and the city has simply built itself around and on top of them: houses climb the lower slopes, roads curve around the craters, and the summits themselves are almost all public parks, free and open, with views that a city planner could never have engineered on purpose.

The youngest and largest of them is Rangitoto, the near-perfect volcanic cone that sits in the middle of the harbour and appears in the background of nearly every photograph taken from the city. Rangitoto is only around 600 years old — young enough that Māori oral history describes watching it form — and its symmetry is so complete that first-time visitors often assume it must be artificial. It isn't. It simply erupted from the seafloor in a single sustained event, or possibly two closely spaced ones, and cooled into the shape the city now uses as its unofficial logo.

Tāmaki Makaurau — the place desired by many

The Māori name for Auckland is Tāmaki Makaurau, generally translated as "Tāmaki desired by many" or "Tāmaki of a hundred lovers" — a reference to how fiercely the isthmus was fought over long before Europeans arrived. The reason is visible on any map: Auckland sits on the narrowest point of the North Island, a strip of land so thin that in places only a few kilometres separate the Waitematā Harbour on the Pacific side from the Manukau Harbour on the Tasman side. Canoes could be portaged across it, giving whoever controlled the isthmus access to both coasts without the long and dangerous sea route around the top of the island.

That strategic value made the volcanic cones themselves valuable. Māori built pā — fortified settlements — on the summits and terraced the slopes for cultivation, and at least thirty-three of the volcanic cones carried a pā at some point. Maungakiekie, known today as One Tree Hill, was the largest of them, with earthwork terracing so extensive it remains visible from the air. By the time Europeans arrived in the early 1800s, though, intertribal conflict fought partly with recently introduced muskets had emptied much of the isthmus, and the land the colonial government purchased in 1840 to found its new capital was, by local accounts, largely uninhabited.

Auckland is the largest Polynesian city on Earth — bigger, by population, than any city in the Pacific Islands themselves.

Auckland today has the largest Polynesian population of any city in the world, New Zealand-born Māori included alongside large Samoan, Tongan, Cook Islands, Niuean, and Fijian communities — the demographic legacy of both the city's Pacific location and decades of Pacific Island migration through the twentieth century. It is a fact that surprises people who arrive expecting a purely European-settler city and find instead one of the most Pacific places on the planet.

The capital that lost its job

Auckland was New Zealand's first capital, declared in 1841 by Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson, who named it after George Eden, Earl of Auckland — a British naval official who, as far as anyone can tell, never once set foot in the place. The choice of site was almost entirely about the isthmus's two harbours and the trade routes they opened up, and for two and a half decades Auckland ran the country.

It did not last. The South Island's gold rushes shifted the colony's population and wealth southward through the 1850s and 60s, and in 1865 the capital was moved to Wellington, chosen largely for its more central location between the two islands. Auckland has never entirely forgiven the demotion, and a certain rivalry with Wellington — genial on the surface, less so a few drinks in — persists to this day. What Auckland kept, and what Wellington never had, was the harbour, and the city built its identity around it instead.

City of Sails

Auckland's council formally adopted "City of Sails" as a civic nickname in 1985, but the reputation long predates the branding. The Waitematā Harbour and the Hauraki Gulf beyond it form one of the most sheltered and varied stretches of sailing water anywhere, dotted with islands close enough for a day trip and open enough for genuine ocean racing, and Aucklanders took to it with an enthusiasm that shows in the numbers: at the nickname's peak the city was estimated to have roughly one boat for every three households, one of the highest per-capita boat ownership rates of any city on Earth.

The city has hosted the America's Cup — sailing's oldest international trophy — multiple times since the late 1990s, rebuilding stretches of the downtown waterfront each time to host the syndicates and the crowds. The Viaduct Harbour, now lined with restaurants and bars a short walk from the CBD, is largely a legacy of that first Cup defence: a working boatyard turned permanently into the city's most fashionable stretch of waterfront.

The bridge, the clip-ons, and the sprawl

For nearly a century after colonial settlement, the only way across the Waitematā Harbour to the North Shore was by ferry. A bridge had been proposed as early as the 1860s, but it took until 1959 for the Auckland Harbour Bridge to finally open, its steel arch spans immediately nicknamed the "coat hanger" for their shape. The bridge was underbuilt from the day it opened — engineers had trimmed the original design from eight lanes to four to save money — and by 1969 two extra lanes had to be bolted onto each side. They were prefabricated in Japan and shipped over in sections, earning them the enduring nickname "Nippon clip-ons," and the bridge has carried the scars of that cost-cutting, and the traffic that followed, ever since.

The bridge opened the North Shore to suburban development almost overnight, and Auckland has been spreading outward in every direction it can ever since. The metro area now sprawls across roughly 1,600 square kilometres for a population of about a million and a half — low-density by the standards of most world cities of its size — a pattern shaped by cheap land, a car-first twentieth century, and a harbour and volcanic field that made the isthmus itself impossible to build on solidly. The tension between that sprawl and a growing appetite for a more compact, transit-connected city is one of the defining civic arguments of Auckland's present moment, visible in the light-rail debates and the City Rail Link tunnel now threading beneath the CBD.

Two harbours, two seas

What ties all of this together — the volcanoes, the portage routes, the sailing, the sprawl — is the same geographic accident: Auckland is one of the very few cities in the world built on an isthmus narrow enough to touch two different oceans. The Waitematā opens east into the Hauraki Gulf and the Pacific; the Manukau opens west into the Tasman Sea. A visitor can stand on the summit of one of the free volcanic cones — Mount Eden or One Tree Hill both do the job — and see water on both horizons at once, the whole logic of the city laid out below in a single turn of the head.
